WASHINGTON (CNN)  -- Secretary of State Hillary Clinton reached an important milestone Wednesday in her quest to pay the debt from her failed 2008 presidential bid: For the first time in eight months, her campaign committee reported having more money in the bank than it owes. Secretary of State Hillary Clinton's campaign committee reported owing $2.3 million in debt at the end of March. On a day most Americans were preoccupied with filing their federal income taxes, Clinton's campaign committee filed finance documents with the Federal Election Commission, reporting a total of $2.3 million in debts at the end of March, compared with $2.6 million in the bank. The nation's top diplomat has been steadily chipping away at unpaid campaign bills since suspending her White House bid in June 2008, when her debt peaked at $25.2 million. That amount covered $12 million owed to vendors, as well as the $13.2 million she loaned her campaign from personal funds. Clinton's campaign was unable to repay that personal loan by the time the Democratic National Convention convened in Denver, Colorado, last August, the deadline mandated by the 2002 McCain-Feingold campaign finance law. The former New York senator was forced to forgive the entire loan amount. Her campaign owed $6.4 million to 16 creditors at the end of November; $5.9 million to five creditors at the end of December; and the current $2.3 million owed to just one creditor at the end of March. That creditor is Penn, Schoen & Berland, a political consulting and polling firm that advised Clinton during her presidential bid. The firm's president, Mark Penn, was Clinton's senior campaign strategist until he stepped down last April amid revelations that he had lobbied on behalf of Colombia for a U.S.-Colombia trade deal that Clinton opposed. Penn remained involved with the campaign. Earlier this year, Clinton and her supporters raced to pay as much of the debt as possible by the time she was confirmed and sworn in as the nation's 67th secretary of state on January 21. As of that date, Clinton became subject to a federal law known as the Hatch Act, which prohibits federal employees from personally soliciting or accepting political contributions. The Hatch Act allows others to keep raising money on Clinton's behalf, without her direct involvement. This week, longtime Clinton ally James Carville, a CNN contributor, sent a fundraising e-mail to Democrats on behalf of Clinton's campaign, requesting contributions of as little as $5 in exchange for a chance to win one of several prizes, including spending a day with former President Bill Clinton. "I won't spend a lot of time trying to convince you to help Hillary," Carville e-mailed. "I know what she means to you, and I'm sure you know how important it is for her to have her campaign pay off all its obligations." It's unclear whether the campaign will use the $2.6 million in the bank to clear its $2.3 million in debts in the short term. Continued fundraising indicates that it will not. Additional operating expenses and other outlays could emerge. Any extra money from the campaign could be donated to political causes or returned to donors. In addition to tapping traditional fundraising, the campaign also generated money by selling or renting various campaign assets to other organizations. Organizations that have rented Clinton's lists include the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, the inaugural committee of then-President-elect Barack Obama, and the William Jefferson Clinton Foundation. Those organizations each paid $274,297. Clinton's political action committee, HillPAC, rented the lists for $822,492. Among the Democratic candidates who have rented Clinton's campaign lists are Arkansas Sen. Blanche Lincoln; Virginia gubernatorial candidate and former Clinton campaign Chairman Terry McAuliffe; New York Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand, who was appointed to fill Clinton's seat; and New York congressional candidate Scott Murphy, who hopes to succeed Gillibrand in the U.S. House.

WASHINGTON (CNN) -- Secretary of State Hillary Clinton reached a significant milestone Wednesday in her ongoing effort to retire the debt from her unsuccessful 2008 presidential campaign: for the first time in eight months, her campaign committee reported holding more cash on hand than it owed in outstanding obligations.

On a day when most Americans were preoccupied with filing their federal income taxes, Clinton's campaign committee submitted finance documents to the Federal Election Commission indicating $2.3 million in debt at the end of March, against $2.6 million in available funds.

The nation's top diplomat has been steadily whittling down her campaign's unpaid bills since suspending her presidential bid in June 2008, at which point her debt had swelled to $25.2 million. That total comprised $12 million owed to various vendors, along with $13.2 million in personal funds she had loaned to her own campaign.

Clinton's campaign was unable to repay that personal loan before the Democratic National Convention convened in Denver, Colorado, last August—the deadline established under the 2002 McCain-Feingold campaign finance law. As a result, the former New York senator was compelled to forgive the loan in its entirety.

The trajectory of her campaign's debt reduction has been notable: $6.4 million owed to 16 creditors at the close of November; $5.9 million owed to five creditors by the end of December; and now just $2.3 million owed to a single creditor as of March's end. That remaining creditor is Penn, Schoen & Berland, a political consulting and polling firm that had advised Clinton throughout her presidential campaign. The firm's president, Mark Penn, served as Clinton's senior campaign strategist until stepping down last April amid revelations that he had lobbied on behalf of Colombia for a U.S.-Colombia trade agreement that Clinton opposed. Despite his departure, Penn continued to be involved with the campaign in other capacities.

Earlier this year, Clinton and her supporters mounted an intensive effort to pay down as much debt as possible before her confirmation and swearing-in as the nation's 67th secretary of state on January 21. From that date forward, Clinton became subject to the federal Hatch Act, which bars federal employees from personally soliciting or accepting political contributions. The law does, however, permit others to continue fundraising on her behalf, without her direct involvement.

This week, longtime Clinton ally James Carville, a CNN contributor, dispatched a fundraising email to Democrats on behalf of Clinton's campaign, soliciting contributions as modest as $5 in exchange for a chance to win various prizes—among them, a day spent with former President Bill Clinton. "I won't spend a lot of time trying to convince you to help Hillary," Carville wrote. "I know what she means to you, and I'm sure you know how important it is for her to have her campaign pay off all its obligations."

Whether the campaign intends to use its $2.6 million in reserves to immediately settle the remaining $2.3 million in debt remains uncertain; the continuation of fundraising efforts suggests otherwise. Additional operating expenses may yet arise, and any surplus funds could ultimately be directed toward political causes or returned to donors.

Clinton's campaign reported raising $938,000 in contributions during the first three months of 2009. Beyond conventional fundraising, the campaign also generated revenue by selling or leasing various campaign assets to other organizations. It received $2.6 million from Clinton's "Friends of Hillary" U.S. Senate campaign committee for the sale of unspecified assets, along with an additional $2.2 million from renting out its lists of campaign supporters.

Organizations that have leased Clinton's donor lists include the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, the presidential inaugural committee of Barack Obama, and the William Jefferson Clinton Foundation—each of which paid $274,297. Clinton's political action committee, HillPAC, paid $822,492 for the same access.

Among the Democratic candidates who have rented Clinton's campaign lists are Arkansas Sen. Blanche Lincoln; Virginia gubernatorial candidate and former Clinton campaign chairman Terry McAuliffe; New York Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand, who was appointed to fill Clinton's vacated Senate seat; and New York congressional candidate Scott Murphy, who hopes to succeed Gillibrand in the House of Representatives.

WASHINGTON (CNN) -- This past Wednesday marked a significant turning point for Secretary of State Hillary Clinton in her ongoing effort to eliminate the financial burden left over from her unsuccessful 2008 presidential campaign. For the first time in eight months, the campaign's bank balance exceeded its outstanding obligations.

According to finance paperwork submitted to the Federal Election Commission on tax filing day, Clinton's campaign committee closed out March with $2.3 million in liabilities, while holding $2.6 million in available cash.

Since ending her presidential run in June 2008, when the campaign's debt reached a staggering $25.2 million, the top U.S. diplomat has gradually worked to pay down what was owed. That original sum included $12 million owed to various vendors along with $13.2 million Clinton had personally loaned to her own campaign.

By the time Democrats gathered for their national convention in Denver last August—the deadline established under the McCain-Feingold campaign finance reform law of 2002—Clinton's campaign still hadn't repaid her personal loan. As a result, the former senator from New York had no choice but to write off the entire loan as a loss.

The debt reduction progressed steadily: $6.4 million owed to 16 different creditors by the end of November, dropping to $5.9 million across five creditors by December's end, and finally shrinking to the current $2.3 million owed to a single creditor as of March.

That remaining creditor is Penn, Schoen & Berland, a polling and political consulting firm that had guided Clinton's campaign strategy. The firm's president, Mark Penn, served as Clinton's chief campaign strategist until his resignation last April, following disclosures that he had lobbied on Colombia's behalf for a trade agreement with the U.S.—a deal Clinton had publicly opposed. Despite stepping down, Penn continued his involvement with the campaign in some capacity.

Clinton and her allies had worked urgently at the start of this year to pay down as much debt as possible before her confirmation and swearing-in as America's 67th secretary of state on January 21. Once she assumed that role, Clinton became bound by the Hatch Act, federal legislation that bars government employees from directly asking for or accepting political donations. However, the law does permit others to fundraise on her behalf, so long as she isn't personally involved in the solicitation.

Just this week, CNN contributor and longtime Clinton supporter James Carville sent out a fundraising appeal to Democratic voters, soliciting donations starting at just $5 for a chance to win prizes—including a day spent with former President Bill Clinton. In his email, Carville wrote: "I won't spend a lot of time trying to convince you to help Hillary. I know what she means to you, and I'm sure you know how important it is for her to have her campaign pay off all its obligations."

Whether the campaign will immediately use its $2.6 million cash reserve to settle the $2.3 million debt remains uncertain, and the fact that fundraising efforts continue suggests it won't happen right away. Additional expenses may still surface down the road. Should any surplus funds remain once debts are cleared, they could either be redirected toward political causes or refunded to original donors.

During the first quarter of 2009, Clinton's campaign brought in $938,000 through contributions. Beyond conventional fundraising methods, the campaign also generated revenue by leasing or selling campaign-related assets to outside organizations. Her Senate campaign committee, "Friends of Hillary," contributed $2.6 million from asset sales, while renting out donor and supporter lists brought in another $2.2 million.

Groups that paid to use Clinton's contact lists include the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, President-elect Barack Obama's inaugural committee, and the William Jefferson Clinton Foundation—each paying $274,297. Clinton's own political action committee, HillPAC, paid $822,492 for list access.

Democratic politicians who have similarly rented these campaign lists include Arkansas Senator Blanche Lincoln, Virginia gubernatorial hopeful and former Clinton campaign chairman Terry McAuliffe, New York Senator Kirsten Gillibrand—who took over Clinton's former Senate seat—and New York congressional candidate Scott Murphy, who is seeking to fill Gillibrand's vacated House seat.

**Clinton's 2008 campaign debt finally erased, FEC filings show**

*By CNN Staff*

WASHINGTON (CNN) — More than four years after Hillary Clinton suspended her bid for the 2008 Democratic presidential nomination, her campaign has finally emerged from the red, according to filings submitted to the Federal Election Commission.

The FEC report shows Clinton's 2008 presidential committee is now debt-free, with cash on hand slightly exceeding the remaining obligations that had lingered on the campaign's books for years — a milestone that closes one of the most persistent financial sagas in recent presidential politics.

At its peak, Clinton's campaign debt topped roughly $25 million, a sum that included more than $13 million she had loaned to her own campaign out of personal funds during the bruising primary battle against then-Senator Barack Obama. The debt became a recurring embarrassment and a talking point for critics who questioned her fundraising operation even as she went on to serve as secretary of state.

"This has been a long time coming," said a former Clinton campaign finance aide familiar with the effort to retire the debt. "It took years of steady, grassroots fundraising, plus help from some very high-profile allies, to finally get this off the books."

According to the FEC filings, the campaign chipped away at the debt gradually through small-dollar online appeals, direct mail solicitations to past donors, and periodic fundraising events. Clinton herself forgave a portion of the money she was owed, while Obama — once the debt became a unifying cause after the bitter primary — headlined joint fundraisers and personally solicited donations from his own network to help pay it down, a gesture widely seen as part of the political rapprochement between the two camps following the 2008 general election.

The filings show the committee reporting cash on hand in the low six figures, alongside zero outstanding debts — the first time the campaign's ledger has shown a positive balance since Clinton ended her primary run in June 2008.

Political analysts say the timing is notable, coming as speculation mounts over whether Clinton will mount another presidential campaign in 2016. A campaign finally free of old debt removes what had been seen as a potential vulnerability — both a symbolic and practical one — should she decide to run again.

"Debt from a losing primary campaign doesn't disqualify anyone, but it's certainly cleaner to start fresh," said one Democratic strategist not affiliated with Clinton's operation. "Donors like to see fiscal discipline, and this puts that whole chapter to rest."

Clinton's political operation declined to comment extensively on the filing, but a spokesperson noted only that "we're grateful to everyone who contributed to closing this out" and that the former secretary of state "is focused on her work through the Clinton Foundation," dismissing further questions about future political plans.

The FEC filing covers the reporting period through the end of the most recent quarter and was submitted in accordance with standard campaign finance disclosure requirements. CNN's review of the filing found no other outstanding obligations tied to the 2008 committee.

With the debt now retired, Clinton's 2008 campaign — once the best-funded operation in Democratic primary history before it was overtaken by Obama's record-breaking fundraising — closes its books having spent more than $230 million over the course of the primary contest.

*CNN's political unit contributed to this report.*

# The Long Road to Zero: Hillary Clinton's Campaign Debt Saga

## A Timeline of Financial Recovery

**June 2008: The Reckoning**

When Hillary Clinton suspended her presidential campaign in June 2008, she left behind a financial trail that stunned political observers: approximately $25.2 million in campaign debt. Of this staggering sum, roughly $13.2 million represented money Clinton had personally loaned her own campaign—a decision that would complicate her path to fiscal recovery in ways few anticipated.

The debt became a symbol of the bruising primary battle against Barack Obama, a contest that stretched deep into the spring and drained resources on both sides. But while Obama's campaign emerged from the primary season financially healthy, Clinton's operation faced a mountain of unpaid vendor bills, consultant fees, and personal loans.

**Summer-Fall 2008: The Fundraising Challenge**

Retiring campaign debt is notoriously difficult once a candidate is no longer actively running. Donors who max out during a campaign often show little enthusiasm for writing checks after the votes have been counted. Clinton's team launched debt-retirement fundraising efforts, hosting events and sending appeals to supporters, but progress was slow.

Complicating matters further was the personal nature of much of the debt. Federal Election Commission rules governing candidate loans created additional pressure—there were limits and complications tied to how quickly and through what means Clinton could be repaid for her personal contributions to the campaign.

**January 2009: A New Complication Emerges**

When President Obama nominated Clinton to serve as Secretary of State, a new legal dimension entered the debt saga: the Hatch Act.

This Depression-era law, designed to prevent federal employees from engaging in certain political activities, cast a shadow over Clinton's ability to continue raising money to pay off her campaign obligations. As a sitting cabinet official, Clinton would face significant restrictions on political fundraising—the very activity she needed to erase her remaining debt.

The timing created a genuine dilemma. Clinton needed to resolve her campaign finances, but assuming her new role as America's chief diplomat meant accepting sharp limits on the fundraising apparatus that might otherwise have continued chipping away at the debt.

**Early 2009: The State Department Transition**

Upon her confirmation as Secretary of State in late January 2009, Clinton effectively stepped back from direct fundraising activities for her campaign debt. The Hatch Act restrictions meant she could no longer personally solicit contributions in the way she had during her post-primary fundraising push.

This didn't mean the debt vanished—it meant the mechanisms for addressing it grew more constrained. Some fundraising could continue through surrogates and campaign staff, but without Clinton's direct involvement, the urgency and effectiveness of these efforts diminished considerably.

**Status in 2009: Debt Persists**

By mid-2009, reports indicated that a significant portion of Clinton's campaign debt remained unresolved. While the exact figures fluctuated in various reports, estimates suggested that several million dollars—including a substantial chunk of the personal loans she had extended to her own campaign—remained outstanding.

The situation highlighted a broader tension in American political life: the collision between electoral politics and governmental service. Clinton's ascension to one of the most powerful positions in government came bundled with new restrictions that, paradoxically, made resolving her past political obligations more difficult.

## The Broader Implications

Clinton's debt saga illustrated systemic issues in campaign finance that extend beyond any single candidate. The difficulty of retiring post-election debt, especially personal loans, has affected numerous candidates across the political spectrum. Her situation, however, gained particular attention due to her prominence and the subsequent complications introduced by her cabinet appointment.
